cards.extra: It is more than a naming trick: every inner instance is tied to an instance of the enclosing class, which is what gives it access to the outer object's members.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Outer { class Inner { int n = 1; } }  // Inner is defined inside Outer
class Demo { Outer.Inner x = new Outer().new Inner(); }

cards.front: What can an inner-class object reach that a separate class cannot?
cards.back: The private members of the enclosing object, with no qualification
cards.extra: The link is implicit and per-object. That access is the actual reason inner classes exist — the book calls it the valuable twist behind the syntax.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Outer { private int secret = 7; class Inner { int read() { return secret; } } }  // no qualification needed
class Demo { int run() { return new Outer().new Inner().read(); } }

cards.front: From outside, how do you name an inner class's type?
cards.extra: The full name includes the enclosing type, which is why two inner classes can share a simple name in different outers.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Outer { class Inner { } }
class Demo { Outer.Inner x = new Outer().new Inner(); }  // type name: OuterClassName.InnerClassName

cards.front: How do you create an inner object from outside the outer class?
cards.extra: The syntax mirrors the dependency: an inner object needs an enclosing instance. Inside the outer class, plain new Inner() borrows this.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Outer { class Inner { } }
class Demo { void run() { Outer outer = new Outer(); Outer.Inner in = outer.new Inner(); } }  // outer.new Inner()

cards.front: What does Outer.this mean inside an inner class?
cards.back: The enclosing instance, not the inner one
cards.extra: Plain this is the inner object. When both have a field of the same name, Outer.this.field is the only way to say which you mean.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Outer { int id = 1; class Inner { int id = 2; int outerId() { return Outer.this.id; } } }
class Demo { int run() { return new Outer().new Inner().outerId(); } }  // 1: Outer.this, not the inner id

cards.front: What is an anonymous inner class?
cards.back: A class declared and instantiated in one expression, with no name
cards.extra: new Runnable() { public void run() {...} } — used for one-off implementations, and the direct ancestor of the lambda syntax that replaced it in most cases.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Greeter { void greet() { System.out.println("hi"); } }
class Demo { void run() { Greeter g = new Greeter() { void greet() { System.out.println("hello"); } }; g.greet(); } }  // no class name
